opus-5.5.text:
Well, the core idea from that work with Marcus Hutter hasn't really changed for me. Intelligence is an agent's ability to achieve goals across a wide range of environments. That universal intelligence measure is a nice formal definition, but it isn't something you can compute. It's a theoretical anchor rather than a practical test.

What's changed is how I think about measuring it in practice. When I wrote the thesis, AI systems were narrow. You'd build something that played chess or recognized digits, and the question of generality was mostly philosophical. Now we have systems that are quite general in some ways, and the measurement problem has become very concrete and urgent.

I've come to think that no single benchmark is going to capture it. Human intelligence isn't one test either; psychologists use broad batteries. So for AGI, I think you need a very large collection of tasks covering the full breadth of cognitive things people can do. Then you ask whether there's anything a typical human can do cognitively that the machine can't. If you keep finding gaps, you're not there yet. When it becomes really hard to find any, that's a strong signal you've reached something like AGI.

The other thing I appreciate more now is that current models are uneven. They're superhuman in some areas, like breadth of knowledge, and surprisingly weak in others, like episodic memory, learning on the fly from a few experiences, or certain kinds of reliable reasoning. So measuring intelligence today is less about one number going up and more about mapping that jagged profile and seeing where the holes are.

r001.rationale: Defines intelligence as achieving goals across a wide range of environments and recommends assessing a broad collection of cognitive tasks.

r002.rationale: Does not discuss environment weighting or its dependence on a reference machine.

r003.rationale: Does not propose human intelligence in human-like environments as an anchor for choosing a reference machine.

r004.rationale: Says the universal intelligence measure cannot be computed, but does not identify Kolmogorov complexity as the reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Dwarkesh. It's a good question, because that thesis was written at a time when the thing we were trying to define barely existed in practice, and now I spend most of my days looking at systems that would have seemed like science fiction back then.

The core idea in the thesis, which Marcus Hutter and I worked on, was pretty abstract. We looked at how people across psychology, philosophy, and AI had defined intelligence, and the common thread was something like: an agent's ability to achieve goals across a wide range of environments. We then tried to make that precise in a mathematical way. You take a huge space of possible environments, you weight them by their complexity using Kolmogorov complexity, and you measure how well an agent does across all of them. Simpler environments get more weight, but you still care about being able to handle the complex ones. It was very much a theoretical object. You couldn't actually compute it.

What I think has held up is the general shape of it. Intelligence as generality of capability, as opposed to performance on any single task, has turned out to be the right framing. When people argued about whether Deep Blue was intelligent, the obvious answer was that it was extraordinarily good at one thing and could do nothing else. That's the distinction the measure captures. And when we think about what we're trying to build at DeepMind, that's still what we mean by AGI: a system that can do essentially all the cognitive tasks a person can do, not a system that's superhuman at one narrow thing.

Where my thinking has changed is on the measurement side. In the thesis, the measure was elegant partly because it sidestepped humans entirely. It was a universal measure, in principle applicable to any agent. But in practice, when you're trying to decide whether a system is at human level, the thing you really want to know is whether it can do the range of things humans do, and humans are actually a very good reference point for that. People have had millions of years of evolution and a lifetime of experience shaping what kinds of problems they can handle. So the practical question becomes: across the full breadth of human cognitive tasks, where are the gaps?

And that leads to the other big shift, which is that I've become much more interested in the breadth and the long tail than in the average. Early on, the natural move was to build benchmarks and track scores. But the current systems are strange. They can do things that would have looked like clear evidence of AGI fifteen years ago, like write working code or pass professional exams, and at the same time they fail at things that a child finds easy. So an average score over some test suite hides exactly the thing you care about. What matters is the shape of the profile. Where are the holes? Are the holes shrinking? If you can find a cognitive task that a typical person can do and the system can't, you don't have AGI yet, more or less by definition. That's a much more adversarial way of thinking about measurement than the thesis had.

I'd also say I underestimated how much things like continual learning and memory would matter. The theoretical measure treated the agent as a fixed thing you evaluate. But a person keeps learning, keeps building on experience over years. Current systems are mostly trained once and then frozen, with a context window bolted on. Whether that counts as a gap in intelligence or just an engineering limitation is a bit of a debate, but I lean towards saying it's a real part of the picture, and any serious measure needs to account for it.

So the summary would be: the definition survived, the idea that it should be a single clean number mostly didn't. What I believe now is that you need a well-defined reference, which for practical purposes is a human, a broad battery of tests that covers the full range of what that reference can do, and a focus on the hardest remaining gaps rather than the headline score. That's less mathematically beautiful than what I wrote in the thesis, but it's a lot more useful for actually answering the question of how close we are.

r001.rationale: It describes intelligence as an agent’s ability to achieve goals across a wide range of environments and distinguishes this from performance on a single task.

r002.rationale: It says environments are weighted by complexity, but does not say that this weighting depends on the choice of reference machine.

r003.rationale: It uses humans as a practical reference for judging systems, but does not propose human intelligence in human-like environments as an anchor for choosing the reference machine in the universal intelligence measure.

r004.rationale: It says the measure could not actually be computed, but does not identify the uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity as the reason.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two things: what we mean by intelligence, and how we measure it in practice. In my thesis, I was trying to make precise the idea that intelligence is an agent’s ability to achieve goals across a wide range of environments. I still think that captures something important. It’s about generality: can you succeed when the situation changes, rather than just perform one particular task extremely well?

But that doesn’t immediately give you a practical test. The mathematical formulation involves a distribution over an infinite space of environments. Once you build a finite evaluation, you have to decide which environments to include, how to weight them, and what resources the agent gets. Those choices matter enormously.

What’s become much more salient with modern systems is the distinction between doing well on a test and having the underlying capability we intended to test. If a system has encountered similar problems during training, a high score may tell you less than you think. I’m more interested in whether it can handle genuinely new problems, learn something unfamiliar, and apply that learning reliably.

So I still find the broad definition useful, but I wouldn’t expect one benchmark number to tell us everything. In practice, you need a range of evaluations, and you need to keep questioning what those evaluations actually establish.

r001.rationale: The response defines intelligence as achieving goals across a wide range of environments and emphasizes success when situations change.

r002.rationale: It says practical evaluations require choices about environments, weighting, and resources, but does not explain that universal intelligence’s environment weighting depends on the choice of reference machine.

r003.rationale: It does not propose anchoring the reference machine using human intelligence in human-like environments.

r004.rationale: It mentions an infinite environment space but does not identify the uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity as a limitation.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the definition from the measurement. The idea behind universal intelligence was to ask: can we give a precise mathematical account of an agent’s ability to achieve goals across a wide range of environments? I still think that captures something important. Intelligence isn’t just being good at chess or doing mathematics. It’s being able to deal with different problems, including ones you haven’t encountered before.

But that doesn’t immediately give you a practical test. In the formal definition, you’re considering an enormous space of possible environments and weighting them by their complexity. You can’t simply implement that and get an intelligence score for a real system. And the choices you make in approximating it matter.

What’s become much more salient with modern AI is how uneven capabilities can be. A system can do something that looks extraordinarily sophisticated and then fail at something a child finds straightforward. So if you compress everything into one number, you can lose precisely the information you need to understand the system.

I’m therefore more interested in a broad collection of evaluations: what can it learn, how well does it generalize, can it solve genuinely unfamiliar problems, and how reliably can it carry out a task? You also have to distinguish what it can do with a little prompting from what it can do with tools, memory, or substantial computation.

So I haven’t abandoned the original abstraction. I think of it as a useful starting point. But the practical question—how do we know what intelligence a particular system has?—requires much more empirical work than the definition itself can provide.

r001.rationale: It describes intelligence as an agent’s ability to achieve goals across a wide range of environments and handle different problems.

r002.rationale: It mentions that approximation choices matter, but does not say that environment weighting depends on the choice of reference machine.

r003.rationale: It does not propose anchoring the reference machine using human intelligence in human-like environments.

r004.rationale: It says the formal definition cannot simply be implemented, but does not identify the uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity as the limitation.
